name: Tibial stress fracture
populations: female athletes with low energy availability
summary: A fatigue crack in the tibia from cumulative loading beyond the bone's remodelling capacity. Posteromedial lesions usually heal with load management; the anterior mid-shaft is a high-risk site.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Low-risk sites: roughly 6–14 weeks (MRI-graded means 42–99 days across sites). High-risk anterior cortex: months, sometimes surgery

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: bony tenderness resolved, pain-free walking, strength and loading tests passed, and radiological healing at high-risk sites

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal bony tenderness with pain on single-leg hop; percussion pain suggests a more severe lesion

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI is the mainstay. Radiographs were abnormal in only 9.8% of athletes imaged at presentation in a 320-case series

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: The tibia accounted for 49.1% of 320 bone-scan-positive stress fractures in athletes

keyFacts.label: Risk status
keyFacts.value: Anterior mid-shaft cortex is high risk (tension side, relatively avascular): delayed union and non-union can occur

overview:
A tibial stress fracture is a fatigue failure of the tibia. It arises when repetitive loads exceed the bone's ability to remove microdamage and remodel, in a generally normal skeleton [r1]. Bone stress injury runs along a continuum from stress reaction, through stress fracture, to complete fracture [r2]. The tibia is the most commonly affected bone in athletes: it accounted for 49.1% of 320 bone-scan-positive stress fractures in one series [r3], and 21.1% of track and field athletes in a 12-month cohort developed a stress fracture, most in the tibia [r4].

Site determines management. Low-risk bone stress injuries typically heal with activity modification followed by progressive loading. Non-weight-bearing immobilisation, medications or surgery are usually reserved for high-risk sites [r1]. The anterior cortex of the tibia is a recognised high-risk site, because tensile forces and relative avascularity predispose to delayed union, non-union and complete fracture [r5]. Contributors include training-load errors and, in athletes, low energy availability and poor bone health [r2,r6]. Recurrence is common, so the cause must be treated as well as the crack [r2]. Return-to-running guidance rests on level IV evidence, so decisions should be shared among clinician, coach and athlete [r7].

epidemiology.text: In 320 athletes with bone-scan-positive stress fractures, the tibia was the most common site (49.1%), followed by the tarsals (25.3%), metatarsals (8.8%), femur (7.2%) and fibula (6.6%); 16.6% of cases were bilateral, and the average time to diagnosis was 13.4 weeks (range 1–78) [r3]. In a 12-month prospective study of 111 track and field athletes aged 17 to 26, the stress fracture incidence was 21.1%, most commonly in the tibia. No measured risk factor predicted stress fractures in men, whereas in women lower bone density, menstrual disturbance, less lean mass in the lower limb, a leg length discrepancy and a lower fat diet were significant, and age at menarche and calf girth were the best independent predictors [r4]. In a case-control study of tibial stress injuries (48 cases, 36 controls), cases had more fat mass, less muscle mass, a tendency for smaller bones, more foot anomalies (56.3% versus 27.8%) and more orthotic use (25% versus 5.6%), with normal bone mineral density in both groups [r8]. In 259 exercising girls and women, 10.8% had a bone stress injury, and the risk rose from about 15–20% with single female athlete triad-related risk factors to 30–50% with combined factors [r9].

intrinsic: Female sex with menstrual disturbance and lower bone density (in female athletes) [r4]
Low energy availability (relative energy deficiency in sport, REDs), including in male athletes [r6]

Combined triad-related factors: BMI below 21.0 kg/m2, oligo- or amenorrhoea, dietary restraint, leanness sport, 12 or more hours of exercise a week and low bone mass; 46.2% of those with 12+ h/week plus leanness sport plus dietary restraint had a bone stress injury [r9]
Less lean mass, more fat mass, a tendency for smaller bones and foot anomalies [r8]
Less lean mass in the lower limb and a leg length discrepancy in female athletes; calf girth and age at menarche were the best independent predictors in women [r4]
Previous bone stress injury, because recurrence is common [r2]
extrinsic: Abrupt increases in training volume or intensity (modifiable); bone load is more amenable to change than bone strength [r2]
High exercise volume: 12 or more hours a week of purposeful exercise in girls and women [r9]
Running-based sports and training; running was the most common sport at the time of stress fracture in athletes [r3]
High impact loading features (tibial acceleration and loading rates) that gait retraining can reduce [r10]

mechanism.summary: A tibial stress fracture develops over weeks, not in one moment. Repetitive running load produces microdamage faster than targeted remodelling can remove it [r1]. Each stride sends an impact load up the tibia at foot contact [r10], and through stance and push-off the shaft bends under ground reaction and calf muscle forces. The anterior mid-shaft is a tension-side site where tensile forces and relative avascularity lead to poor healing [r5].
sequence: Training load climbs quickly, or recovery and energy intake are inadequate [r2,r6].
At each foot contact the ground reaction force sends an impact load up the tibia; higher tibial acceleration and loading rates are linked with tibial stress fracture [r10].
Through midstance and push-off the tibial shaft bends. The anterior mid-shaft is on the tension side, with relatively poor blood supply [r5].
Microdamage accumulates and resorption outpaces formation, so the cortex weakens locally [r1].
A stress reaction follows: periosteal and then marrow oedema on MRI, with pain on loading [r11].
Continued loading produces a cortical fracture line, a stress fracture; at the anterior cortex the crack may not heal [r12,r5].
If loading persists, the fracture can progress to a complete fracture or non-union [r2,r5].

variants.name: Posteromedial or distal tibial lesion (usually low risk)
variants.description: Posteromedial and distal tibial lesions are generally treated as low risk (clinical convention; the anterior cortex and medial malleolus are the named high-risk tibial sites [r5]). Low-risk sites typically heal with activity modification and progressive loading [r1]. Diffuse border pain at the milder end overlaps with medial tibial stress syndrome [r11].

variants.name: Anterior mid-shaft cortex (high risk)
variants.description: A named high-risk site: tensile forces and relative avascularity predispose to delayed union and non-union, so it needs aggressive management [r5]. Outcomes of conservative and operative treatment are less successful than at low-risk sites [r13].

variants.name: Medial malleolus
variants.description: The medial malleolus is also a high-risk tibial site and should be considered with distal medial tibial pain [r5].

variants.name: Bilateral or multiple stress fractures
variants.description: Bilateral involvement occurred in 16.6% of athletes in a large series, which should prompt a search for a systemic cause such as low energy availability [r3,r6].

anatomy.text: The tibia is the main weight-bearing bone of the lower leg. Its anterior border (crest) lies directly under the skin and the anterior mid-shaft cortex is a tension-side site in bending, with relatively poor blood supply, which helps to explain its poor healing [r5]. The calf muscles (soleus and gastrocnemius) share the load that the tibia carries, so their strength and endurance matter for tibial bone stress injuries [r2]. The fibula lies lateral to the tibia and accounted for 6.6% of stress fractures in one series [r3].

structures.name: Anterior mid-shaft cortex
structures.role: Tension-side cortex in bending; relatively avascular, which makes it a high-risk site [r5]

structures.name: Posteromedial cortex
structures.role: Common site for tibial bone stress injuries, usually low risk and managed with load modification [r1]

structures.name: Periosteum and marrow
structures.role: Respond to bone stress with periosteal and marrow oedema before a cortical line forms [r11]

structures.name: Soleus and gastrocnemius
structures.role: Plantarflex the ankle and share load with the tibia; calf strengthening is advised for tibial bone stress injuries [r2]

structures.name: Fibula and interosseous membrane
structures.role: Share load and stabilise the tibia; fibular stress fractures can coexist [r3]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Bone stress injury occurs when excessive repetitive loads are applied to a generally normal skeleton, and an imbalance in bone metabolism favours microdamage accumulation over its removal and replacement through targeted remodelling [r1]. The risk of microdamage accumulation depends on the load applied and on the bone's ability to resist it; of the two, load is the more amenable to intervention [r2]. The injury moves along a continuum from stress reaction to stress fracture to complete fracture [r2]. On MRI, tibial stress lesions progress from periosteal oedema, through marrow involvement, to a frank cortical fracture line, and MRI relates more closely to symptoms than bone scan [r11]. A five-grade classification describes the injury as asymptomatic stress reaction on imaging (I), pain without a fracture line (II), non-displaced fracture (III), displaced fracture (IV) or non-union (V) [r12].

Healing potential depends on location. Sites under tension, such as the anterior tibial cortex, have a relatively poor blood supply, and tensile forces oppose healing, so they carry a higher risk of delayed union, non-union and progression to complete fracture [r5]. Systemic factors set the threshold: in athletes with low energy availability, bone stress injury rates rise as risk factors accumulate [r9,r6].

structures.name: Tibial cortex at the injury site
structures.effect: Microdamage accumulation, a cortical fracture line, then healing by remodelling if load is managed [r1,r12]

structures.name: Periosteum and marrow
structures.effect: Periosteal oedema and then marrow oedema on MRI [r11]

structures.name: Anterior mid-shaft cortex
structures.effect: High-risk site with tensile loading and relative avascularity; delayed union or non-union may follow [r5]

structures.name: Fibula and adjacent bones
structures.effect: Can be affected at the same time; bilateral lesions occurred in 16.6% of athletes [r3]

muscles.name: Calf complex (soleus, gastrocnemius)
muscles.effect: Lower lean mass is associated with tibial stress injury, and calf girth was an independent predictor in women; strengthening the calf is advised to reduce bone load [r8,r4,r2]

muscles.name: Hip abductors and trunk
muscles.effect: A higher step rate reduced peak hip adduction as well as tibial loading in a trial of healthy runners, so proximal control influences loading [r14]

muscles.name: Foot intrinsic muscles
muscles.effect: Foot anomalies were more common in cases than in controls; foot intrinsic strengthening is advised for metatarsal rather than tibial injuries [r8,r2]

muscles.name: Pain-related changes
muscles.effect: MTSS-type and stress fracture-specific data on muscle inhibition, spasm or atrophy were not found in the sources reviewed.

cellular.description: Repeated submaximal loading creates microcracks in the cortex faster than they are removed [r1].
Targeted remodelling is outpaced: resorption exceeds formation locally, which weakens the cortex [r1,r2].
Periosteal and marrow oedema appear on MRI as the bone responds to the damage [r11].
A cortical fracture line forms; with load reduced and then progressed, remodelling repairs it. In 320 athletes the mean time to recovery was 12.8 weeks (range 2–96) [r3].

systems.effect: Low energy availability produces deleterious health and performance outcomes in female and male athletes, and bone stress injury rates rose from about 15–20% with single triad-related risk factors to 30–50% with combined factors [r6,r9].
A tendency for smaller bones, less lean mass and more fat mass were found in tibial stress injury cases, with normal bone mineral density [r8].
Impact loading rates and tibial acceleration relate to tibial stress fracture; gait retraining lowers them [r10,r14].
Long periods out of training, fear of reinjury and under-fuelling to maintain body composition can drive recurrence; screen and address these with the athlete and coach.

grading.system: Kaeding and Miller stress fracture classification (grade, location, imaging modality) with site risk [r12,r5]

grades.description: Asymptomatic stress reaction seen on imaging only [r12].
grades.prognosis: Usually settles with load adjustment; imaging finding only

grades.description: Pain with no fracture line on imaging [r12].
grades.prognosis: Low-risk sites usually heal with activity modification and progressive loading [r1]
Longer healing; at high-risk sites such as the anterior cortex, protected weight-bearing or surgery may be needed [r1,r5]
Orthopaedic management is usually required (clinical practice)
Surgical review; non-union is a recognised complication at high-risk sites [r5]

timeframes.summary: Healing time depends on site and severity. In a meta-analysis of non-operatively treated bone stress injuries graded by MRI, mean time to return to sport was 41.7, 70.1, 84.3 and 98.5 days for grades 1–4 across all sites, and cortical-rich sites such as the tibia healed faster than trabecular-rich sites [r15]. The anterior cortex is high risk and may take much longer [r5].

healing.description: Remove impact load; walking pain settles and bony tenderness starts to fall
Cortical repair under protected, then progressive, loading [r15]
Calf, hip and trunk strength; graded running after criteria are met [r7]

healing.phase: Return to full training and sport
healing.description: Intensity, speed and sport-specific load reintroduced; monitor for recurrence [r2]

healing.phase: Prolonged protection at a high-risk site
healing.description: Anterior cortex lesions may need months of protection, imaging follow-up and sometimes surgery [r5,r1]

milestones.label: Pain-free walking
milestones.note: Typical clinical target; criteria, not the calendar, decide

milestones.label: Bony tenderness resolved
milestones.note: One of the five components to check before running [r7]

milestones.label: Start walk–run intervals
milestones.note: After strength, functional and loading tests are passed [r7]

milestones.label: Mean return to sport, MRI grade 2–3 (all sites)
Radiological healing at a high-risk site
milestones.note: Needed before running for high-risk lesions [r7]

timeframes.returnToSport: Low-risk lesions: typically 6–14 weeks (MRI-graded means 42–99 days across sites). High-risk anterior cortex lesions: months, with radiological healing required. Return is criteria-based [r15,r7].

symptoms: Insidious, localised shin pain that comes on with running and eases with rest in the early stage [r11]
Progression over days to weeks to pain on walking and, in severe cases, at rest and at night [r11]
Pain that builds with each session and no longer settles within hours of stopping
A recent rise in running volume or intensity, a change of surface, or a period of low energy intake
Occasionally both legs affected (16.6% bilateral in a 320-case series) [r3]
signs: Focal bony tenderness over the fracture site, on the anterior crest or posteromedial border
Pain on single-leg hop or on direct or indirect percussion, which correlated with more severe tibial stress lesions on MRI [r11]
Localised swelling, warmth or thickening of the cortex in longer-standing cases
Normal neurovascular examination in uncomplicated cases

subjective: Pain pattern: localised, load-related pain versus diffuse medial shin pain; night pain or pain on walking suggests more advanced bone stress [r11]
Training load: weekly volume, intensity, surfaces, footwear and any block of increased training in the previous 2–6 weeks
Energy availability and menstrual history: dietary restriction, missed periods, previous fractures, and screening with the REDs Clinical Assessment Tool [r6]
Previous bone stress injuries, because recurrence is common [r2]
Medications, vitamin D and calcium intake, family history of osteoporosis or fractures
Sport, level, upcoming events and what the athlete is willing to change
observation: Gait, running mechanics and foot posture; leg length and alignment [r4]
Calf and thigh bulk compared with the other side [r8]
Local swelling, skin changes and limp
palpation: Map focal bony tenderness along the tibia, separating the anterior crest from the posteromedial border
Check for periosteal thickening or a palpable step at the site in long-standing cases
Compare with diffuse border tenderness over 5 cm or more, which fits MTSS instead [r11]
rangeOfMotion: Ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, subtalar and hip rotation, as contributing factors
Painful end-range loading of the tibia is unusual; pain on ankle range alone suggests another cause
strength: Single-leg calf raise endurance on both sides; weakness is common after weeks off running
Hip abductor and external rotator strength
functional: Single-leg hop on the spot or for distance: reproduction of focal tibial pain suggests a bone stress injury [r16]
Walking tolerance and a short jog on a treadmill with pain rating (only when walking is pain-free)

specialTests.name: Single-leg hop test (pain provocation)
specialTests.purpose: Provoke focal pain from a bone stress injury
specialTests.procedure: The athlete hops repeatedly on the symptomatic leg. Ask about the location and severity of pain and compare with the pain experienced when running.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of focal tibial pain. Pain with single-leg hop is used as a clinical parameter in bone stress injury trials, but accuracy figures were not found in the sources reviewed [r16].

specialTests.name: Percussion test (direct or indirect)
specialTests.purpose: Identify more severe tibial stress lesions
specialTests.procedure: Tap over the tender tibial segment, or percuss the heel or tibial tuberosity to transmit force along the shaft.
specialTests.positive: Pain on direct or indirect percussion, which correlated with more severe tibial stress injuries on MRI. Accuracy figures were not stated [r11].

specialTests.name: Focal palpation of the tibia
specialTests.purpose: Localise the injury and separate it from diffuse border pain
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the whole shaft with firm thumb pressure, mapping the extent of tenderness and noting any pinpoint site.
specialTests.positive: Localised bony tenderness, together with pain on daily walking, correlated with more severe tibial lesions on MRI [r11]. Diffuse tenderness of 5 cm or more points to MTSS.

specialTests.name: Fulcrum test
specialTests.purpose: Stress the tibial shaft to reproduce pain
specialTests.procedure: Place the forearm under the mid-shaft of the supported leg and apply gentle downward pressure at the knee and ankle ends, as a lever.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of focal pain at the fracture site. Accuracy was not found in the sources reviewed; use it as a provocation test only.

clinicalRules.name: High-risk versus low-risk site
clinicalRules.description: Classify the lesion by location. The anterior tibial cortex and the medial malleolus are high-risk tibial sites that need aggressive management; posteromedial lesions are usually low risk [r5,r1].

clinicalRules.name: REDs Clinical Assessment Tool (version 2)
clinicalRules.description: A tool to help detect and diagnose REDs from accumulated severity and risk stratification, with associated training and competition recommendations [r6].

clinicalRules.name: Return-to-running components
clinicalRules.description: Five components before running after a tibial bone stress injury: resolution of bony tenderness, pain-free walking, radiological healing in high-risk lesions, strength, functional and loading tests, and identification of contributing factors. This is level IV evidence [r7].

outcomeMeasures.name: Numeric pain rating scale (0–10) at hop and run
outcomeMeasures.use: Track load tolerance and response to progression

outcomeMeasures.name: Single-leg calf raise endurance and hop symmetry
outcomeMeasures.use: Strength and loading capacity before running [r7]

outcomeMeasures.name: REDs Clinical Assessment Tool
outcomeMeasures.use: Risk stratification of energy availability and bone health [r6]

imaging.indication: First-line for focal pain, though often normal early; useful to look for a cortical line or periosteal reaction
imaging.findings: In 320 athletes, radiographs were taken in 43.4% at presentation and were abnormal in only 9.8%, so a normal film does not exclude a stress fracture [r3]. At the anterior cortex a transverse lucent line signals a high-risk fracture.

imaging.indication: The mainstay for diagnosing and grading bone stress injury; use when focal tenderness, hop pain or night pain suggests a stress lesion [r17,r11]
imaging.findings: Periosteal oedema, then marrow oedema, then a cortical fracture line. Higher MRI grade was associated with a longer time to return to sport [r11,r15].

imaging.indication: Define the fracture line and monitor healing at high-risk sites
imaging.findings: Cortical lucent line, sclerosis and bridging; radiological healing is expected before running for high-risk lesions [r7]

imaging.indication: Rarely needed now that MRI is available
imaging.findings: Sensitive but less specific, and MRI relates more closely to symptoms in runners [r11]

differentials.name: Medial tibial stress syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Diffuse tenderness over 5 cm or more of the posteromedial border, no focal point tenderness, hop test usually negative; the milder end of the same continuum [r11].

differentials.name: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Pain and tightness build at a predictable point in exercise and settle within minutes of rest; no bony tenderness [r17].

differentials.name: Tibia and fibula shaft fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Acute traumatic onset, deformity, inability to weight-bear.

differentials.name: Fibular stress fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Lateral shin pain with tenderness over the fibula; 6.6% of stress fractures in one series [r3].

differentials.name: Soleus strain
differentials.distinguishing: Muscle belly pain with resisted plantarflexion in knee flexion; no bony tenderness.

differentials.name: Bone tumour or infection
differentials.distinguishing: Constant pain unrelated to load, night pain, systemic features, or a mass; refer for urgent imaging.

redFlags: Focal tenderness on the anterior mid-shaft or a transverse lucent line on imaging: a high-risk lesion. Stop impact loading and refer urgently to a sports physician or orthopaedic surgeon [r5].
Sudden severe pain, inability to weight-bear or deformity: possible complete fracture. Send to the emergency department.
Constant pain at rest or night, fever, unexplained weight loss or a mass: consider tumour or infection and arrange urgent imaging and medical review.
No improvement or worsening after 6–12 weeks of correct offloading: repeat imaging for delayed union or non-union and refer [r5].
Severe, escalating pain with a tense swollen leg after a fracture or direct injury: possible acute compartment syndrome. This is an emergency; refer to the emergency department immediately.
Amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea, disordered eating, multiple or recurrent bone stress injuries: screen for REDs and refer to a sports physician and dietitian [r6].

management.principles: Management is guided by the site and the risk of healing complications. Low-risk bone stress injuries typically heal with activity modification followed by progressive loading, while non-weight-bearing immobilisation, medications or surgery are usually limited to high-risk sites [r1]. Address the causes (training load, energy availability, bone health, mechanics), because recurrence is common [r2]. Evidence for specific treatments is limited, and return to running rests on level IV evidence; decisions should be shared among clinician, coach and athlete [r7].

medical.name: Activity modification with symptom-guided relative rest (low-risk sites)
medical.description: Stop impact loading that provokes pain, keep non-impact fitness, then progress loading in stages. Most low-risk bone stress injuries heal this way [r1], and more than 90% of athletes returned to sport after non-operative treatment in a meta-analysis of MRI-graded injuries [r15].

medical.name: Protected or non-weight-bearing immobilisation (high-risk sites)
medical.description: Prolonged protection, a boot or crutches, and imaging follow-up for the anterior cortex or other high-risk lesions, under specialist guidance [r1,r5].

medical.name: Pneumatic leg brace
medical.description: In a randomised trial of 18 athletes with tibial stress fractures, those fitted with an Aircast pneumatic brace returned to full activity in 21 ± 2 days versus 77 ± 7 days with rest and gradual return [r18]. The trial was small and the comparison was with rest alone.

medical.name: Surgery (for example intramedullary nailing)
medical.description: Reserved for high-risk lesions when conservative treatment fails, or for complete fracture or non-union [r1,r13]. No comparative trials of surgical technique were identified in the sources reviewed.

medical.name: Nutrition and endocrine review
medical.description: Correct low energy availability, review menstrual function and vitamin D and calcium status, and refer to a sports physician and dietitian when REDs is suspected [r6,r2].

medical.name: Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS)
medical.description: No effect on MRI grade, marrow oedema or clinical measures at 4 weeks in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 23 people with lower limb bone stress injuries [r16].

medical.name: Simple analgesia
medical.description: Paracetamol for night or rest pain. Avoid using analgesia to push through training, because pain is the guide to loading (clinical convention).

physio.name: Criteria-based progressive loading and graded return to running
physio.description: Resolve bony tenderness and walking pain, build calf and trunk capacity, then add walk–run intervals, progressing distance before speed with symptom provocation as the main guide [r7,r2].

physio.name: Calf strengthening
physio.description: Strengthening the calf is advised for tibial bone stress injuries to reduce the load carried by the bone [r2]. Lean mass was lower in cases than in controls [r8].

physio.name: Gait retraining
physio.description: A cue to raise step rate by 7.5% produced an 8.6% increase, cut vertical loading rates by about 18–19% and reduced peak hip adduction in 30 at-risk healthy runners [r14]. Real-time tibial accelerometer feedback lowered tibial acceleration by nearly 50% in 10 runners [r10]. Effects on stress fracture recurrence have not been shown.

physio.name: Cross-training with non-impact exercise
physio.description: Cycling, pool running and upper body or core work to keep fitness during offloading.

physio.name: Education on load, fuelling and recurrence
physio.description: Explain the bone-loading model, review training plans and energy intake, and agree pain rules before running resumes. Recurrence is common without addressing causes [r2].

education: A stress fracture is a crack from repeated load. It heals when load is managed, but it will not heal if you keep running through pain.
Pain is the guide: if focal pain returns or worsens, stop and be reviewed.
The location matters. Some sites heal reliably; the front of the shin is a high-risk site and needs closer follow-up.
Eat enough for the training you do. Low energy intake, missed periods and repeated stress fractures are linked [r6].
Return to running is gradual and passes through checkpoints for tenderness, walking, strength and hopping [r7].
Fix the causes, not just the crack, because stress fractures often recur [r2].

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based. Protect the bone while the fracture heals, rebuild strength and capacity without impact, then reintroduce running in graded steps and finally full training. Return to running after a tibial bone stress injury is guided by five components: resolution of bony tenderness, pain-free walking, radiological healing for high-risk lesions, strength, functional and loading tests, and identification of contributing factors; this guidance is level IV evidence [r7]. Timeframes below apply to low-risk lesions; high-risk lesions take longer and follow specialist instructions. Dosages are typical clinical ranges. As a working rule, keep pain at 3/10 or less during exercise and settled by the next morning (clinical convention).

stages.name: Protect and unload
goals: Keep fitness and strength without impact
Start addressing energy intake and training plan
precautions: Follow imaging and specialist advice for high-risk lesions [r5]
Use crutches or a boot if walking is painful
Stop and review if focal pain at rest or night pain develops

exercises.name: Cycling or aqua-jogging
exercises.dosage: 30–45 min, 4–5 days a week at a pain-free effort
exercises.cues: Match the intensity of a normal run to keep fitness

exercises.name: Seated calf raise (light, only if pain-free)

progressionCriteria: Marked reduction in bony tenderness on palpation
For high-risk lesions: clinician clearance with imaging showing healing [r7]

stages.name: Restore strength and capacity
goals: Single-leg calf raise endurance close to the other side
Hip and trunk control on one leg
precautions: Increase load only when symptoms are 3/10 or less and settle by the next morning
No running until the tenderness criteria are met [r7]

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–15, 3 s up and 3 s down, 3 days a week; progress with load

progressionCriteria: Single-leg calf raise endurance within about 90% of the other side (clinical convention)
Pain-free double-leg hopping on the spot

stages.name: Graded return to running
goals: Build to 30 min of continuous running
Raise step rate and run softly
precautions: Progress distance before speed, hills or intervals [r7]
Step back if pain exceeds 3/10 or persists into the next morning
High-risk lesions need imaging evidence of healing before running [r7]

exercises.name: Walk–run intervals
exercises.dosage: Alternate days, for example 1 min run and 2 min walk × 8, increasing the run share when criteria are met
exercises.cues: Easy effort on flat, even ground

exercises.name: Step-rate cue
exercises.dosage: Raise cadence by about 5–10% with a metronome during runs initially [r14]

exercises.name: Single-leg hop on the spot
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10 each leg once criteria are met

progressionCriteria: Run 30 min continuously with pain 3/10 or less on two consecutive runs and no pain the next morning

stages.name: Return to training and sport
goals: Prevent recurrence through load monitoring and fuelling
precautions: Increase volume or intensity, not both, in one week; gradual steps, for example about 10% a week (a common clinical convention that is not well validated)
Repeat REDs screening if training load rises sharply

exercises.name: Progressive running volume, then speed and hills
exercises.dosage: Add distance first, then strides, hills and intervals over several weeks

exercises.name: Jump squats and hops
exercises.dosage: 3 × 5–8, twice a week with full recovery

exercises.name: Heavy single-leg calf raise and split squat
Sport-specific drills
exercises.dosage: Cutting, acceleration and sport drills added in steps

exercises.name: Weekly load and fuelling review
exercises.dosage: Once a week with athlete and coach

progressionCriteria: Full training week without next-day tenderness
Calf raise endurance and hop symmetry about 90% (clinical convention)
Contributing factors addressed and a prevention plan in place [r7]

criteria: Resolution of bony tenderness on palpation [r7]
Evidence of radiological healing in high-risk lesions [r7]
Strength, functional and loading tests passed, for example single-leg calf raise and hop symmetry about 90% (clinical convention) [r7]
Contributing factors identified and addressed (training load, energy availability, mechanics) [r7,r2]
Shared decision between clinician, coach and athlete [r7]
tests: Single-leg hop for pain and symmetry
30 min graded running test with pain rating
Radiograph, CT or MRI follow-up for high-risk lesions

prognosis: Most athletes return to sport after non-operative treatment: more than 90% in a meta-analysis of 16 MRI-graded studies (560 bone stress injuries), with mean times to return of 41.7 to 98.5 days across grades 1–4 and faster healing at cortical-rich sites such as the tibia [r15]. In an earlier series the mean recovery time was 12.8 weeks (range 2–96) [r3]. Bone stress injuries tend to recur, which is why causes must be addressed [r2]. High-risk anterior cortex lesions can progress to delayed union, non-union or complete fracture, and the outcomes of both conservative and operative treatment are described as less successful than for low-risk sites [r5,r13].
prevention: Increase running load gradually and monitor symptoms; load is more amenable to modification than bone strength [r2].
Screen for low energy availability and bone health in athletes, including men, and treat it early [r6,r9].
Strengthen the calf and build lean mass; both are associated with tibial stress injury [r2,r8].
Consider gait retraining (a step-rate increase of about 7.5%) for runners with high impact loading; it lowers loading rates but has not been shown to prevent stress fractures [r14,r10].
Review risk in female runners with menstrual disturbance or low bone density [r4].
clinicalPearls: Focal bony tenderness with pain on hopping is a bone stress injury until proven otherwise. Diffuse border tenderness over 5 cm points to MTSS [r11].
Site decides the plan. The anterior mid-shaft tibia is a high-risk site; do not manage it like shin splints [r5].
A normal radiograph does not exclude a stress fracture: films were abnormal in only 9.8% of athletes imaged at presentation [r3]. Use MRI when suspicion is high [r17].
Ask about periods, eating and energy availability in every athlete with a bone stress injury, including men [r6].
Recurrence is common. Fix the cause, not just the crack [r2].
Delay to diagnosis averaged 13.4 weeks in a classic series; earlier recognition shortens time off running [r3].

animation.title: How a tibial stress fracture develops

captions.text: A distance runner is deep into a high-mileage block with little recovery.
At every foot strike an impact load travels up the tibia.
Through stance and push-off the shaft bends under ground reaction and calf forces.
The anterior mid-shaft takes the tension, and its blood supply is relatively poor.
Over weeks, microdamage outpaces repair and localised shin pain builds.
Zooming into the right shin, viewed from the front.

actions.label: Heals with offloading, then progressive load

captions.text: From the front, the anterior mid-shaft of the tibia is the high-risk site.
Repeated bending loads the anterior cortex in tension.
The bone shows a stress reaction as microdamage accumulates.
The periosteum and marrow become inflamed, and loading hurts.
A crack crosses the cortex: a stress fracture.
At this site healing can stall, so delayed union and complete fracture are risks.
With offloading then progressive loading, the bone can heal.
Healthy cortical bone: microdamage is removed and replaced as it forms.
Repetitive running load strains the cortex.
Microcracks accumulate faster than the bone can repair them.
Osteoclast resorption outpaces osteoblast formation locally.
A stress reaction: periosteal and marrow oedema, with pain on loading.
A crack crosses the cortex: a stress fracture.
With load reduced, then progressed, remodelling repairs the crack.
